practicalQuestion: During a seven-day travel period with two competitions, limited food access, and athletes with different playing-time demands, how should performance nutrition prioritize and individualize fueling, hydration, recovery, and supplement decisions while protecting sleep and gastrointestinal tolerance?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate roster with high-minute, low-minute, and returning athletes
decisionContext.outcome: Create an operational nutrition plan that supports readiness across subgroups
decisionContext.constraints: Fixed travel and hotel meals; limited refrigeration; variable minutes and sweat response; supplement and clinical decisions require appropriate review

evidenceConfidence.rationale: Team-sport sources agree on scaling carbohydrate to the work done, refuelling early after competition, food first, and caution with most supplements. No source tests a seven-day collegiate travel nutrition plan or the integrated decision process. The main practical source, the UEFA statement, describes itself as expert opinion (level 5 evidence). Other evidence comes from elite male soccer, rugby and Australian football, a two-player biopsy report, and small laboratory studies. Polyphenol recovery evidence and hydration-glycogen evidence are in unresolved tension. Treat everything below as options, not a recommendation.

dimensions.sourceReview: Sources are an elite football expert statement (self-rated level 5 expert opinion), narrative and systematic reviews with meta-analyses, a two-player muscle biopsy case report, and observational travel and load cohorts. Every claim is checked against original text.
dimensions.directness: Indirect for the integrated question. UEFA addresses congested fixtures, travel and food hygiene as expert guidance, but no source studies a congested travel week with fixed hotel meals and limited refrigeration.
dimensions.consistency: Consistent on matching carbohydrate to demand and on food first. Mixed on polyphenol recovery benefit and on whether dehydration impairs glycogen resynthesis; the hydration meta-analysis pooled result was not significant.
dimensions.transferability: Low to moderate. Populations are mostly professional or elite male soccer, rugby league or union, and Australian football players, plus laboratory samples. Collegiate, female, and returning athletes are not directly studied.

bottomLine.text: The evidence is limited and indirect, so these are options rather than a tested plan. Expert guidance supports carbohydrate scaled to each athlete's minutes and load, food first, and early post-competition carbohydrate, protein and fluid when the next competition is days away. Most supplements look low value and belong in individual review. Travel scheduling has more support for protecting sleep than diet-based tactics.

actions.title: Option: tier fueling by minutes and load
actions.text: Players with more match minutes accumulated more weekly load in one professional soccer team. The UEFA expert statement suggests 6 to 8 g/kg/day carbohydrate across the 48 to 72 hours between congested fixtures and, drawing on a two-game week study, on the day before, day of and day after a match, while noting players often eat closer to 4 g/kg. A rugby league review suggests players may need about 6 to 8 g/kg/day but notes data may be insufficient for sport-specific advice. In two Australian football players, the one who played more minutes and took no in-game carbohydrate used more glycogen, but the authors note minutes, distance and starting glycogen also differed. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): one option is larger carbohydrate portions and in-game carbohydrate for high-minute athletes, with low-minute athletes' intake matched to their actual compensatory training.

actions.title: Option: fixed post-competition recovery routine
actions.text: UEFA suggests targeting about 1 g/kg/h carbohydrate for 4 hours after a match and notes sports foods can help when appetite is low or food is sourced away from home. A rugby league review suggests 1.0 to 1.5 g/kg carbohydrate plus 0.25 to 0.55 g/kg protein within 0 to 2 hours. The hydration review's introduction cites earlier work reporting about 40% glycogen restoration in the first hour with 1 to 1.2 g/kg/h. On fluid, UEFA states normal eating and drinking usually restores euhydration; the hydration review's authors suggest poor rehydration may raise glycogen use when high-intensity work is needed on consecutive days, but their pooled hydration analysis was not significant. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): pre-pack shelf-stable carbohydrate and protein options for the bus or hotel, given limited refrigeration.

actions.title: Option: protect gastrointestinal tolerance
actions.text: UEFA advises an easily digestible pre-match meal, putting comfort ahead of rigid carbohydrate targets, and practising all match nutrition strategies, including sports foods, in training before competition. A cyclist study cited by the rugby league review found less upper gastrointestinal distress with sucrose than glucose after glycogen-depleting exercise. Nitrate can cause minor gastrointestinal upset, and some antioxidants such as NAC may cause gastrointestinal discomfort and diarrhoea. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): avoid introducing new supplements or products during the travel week.

actions.title: Option: keep supplements narrow and reviewed
actions.text: Food first is the expert position, and whole-team supplement plans call for extreme caution. If caffeine is used, a meta-analysis advises caution above 6 mg/kg because those doses showed no added benefit in a small number of studies and may raise side-effect risk; a rugby league review lists sleep disturbance among possible side effects. Antioxidant supplements did not meaningfully reduce soreness, tart cherry did not change soreness, function or inflammation in rugby league players, and UEFA states evidence does not support tart cherry in football. Melatonin was not ergogenic, its sourcing and side effects need consideration, and pharmacological sleep aids should be doctor-overseen. UEFA notes a broad multivitamin can support intake when food choice and quality are limited.

actions.title: Option: protect sleep through scheduling
actions.text: Overnight long-haul travel caused about 3 hours of in-flight sleep loss in professional rugby union players, physical performance stayed impaired for 3 mornings after arrival, and the authors recommend arriving more than 3 days before matches after such travel. In national-team footballers, daytime arrivals (11 AM to 5 PM) were least detrimental to perceived sleep and fatigue. UEFA reports that diet-based jet lag methods are not unequivocally supported and that sleep hygiene should come first. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): avoid placing large or late meals, or caffeine, where they could compete with sleep opportunities.

actions.title: Option: plan hydration and food handling for travel
actions.text: UEFA describes planning around individual sweat losses and warns that food storage and preparation at postmatch buffets, changing rooms or the team bus can cause serious gastrointestinal illness, pointing to cleaning, chilling, cooking and cross-contamination controls. A rugby league review, citing ACSM guidance, advises keeping fluid losses under 2% of body mass. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): with limited refrigeration, favour shelf-stable foods and drinks for transport and avoid holding perishable recovery food.

monitoring.label: Minutes and load
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): track each athlete's match minutes and training load across the week so fueling tiers follow actual work, since load rose with playing time in the cited cohort.

monitoring.label: Fluid status
monitoring.text: UEFA describes individual sweat-loss planning, and a rugby league review citing ACSM guidance advises limiting fluid loss to under 2% of body mass and drinking about 1.25 to 1.5 L per kg lost after exercise. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): pre and post body mass checks are one practical way to estimate loss.

monitoring.label: Gut symptoms
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): ask athletes about gastrointestinal symptoms around pre-competition and recovery feeds, and adjust carbohydrate type and timing.

monitoring.label: Sleep after travel
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): monitor sleep and fatigue on the night and days after arrival, since travel timing affected these outcomes in the cited cohorts.

guardrails.text: Supplement, melatonin, and other clinical decisions require appropriate medical and dietitian review. UEFA calls for extreme caution with whole-team supplement plans and says pharmacological sleep interventions should be overseen by a medical doctor. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): the WADA team rule cited by that source does not map directly to collegiate rules, so confirm with compliance staff.

UEFA suggests moving injured players back toward normal training nutrition as they progress toward return to play. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): nutrition planning does not clear anyone for play; progression and clearance decisions stay with the treating clinicians.

The gram-per-kilogram targets come from an expert-opinion statement and from a review of young professional male rugby league players that notes data may be insufficient for sport-specific recommendations. Use them as starting ranges, not prescriptions.

limitations.text: Populations are mostly elite or professional male soccer, rugby league, rugby union, and Australian football players. The glycogen data come from only 2 Australian football forwards. Collegiate and female athletes are not directly studied.
The UEFA statement, which supplies most practical targets, rates itself as expert opinion evidence.

Hydration and glycogen evidence rests on small, heterogeneous studies with low quality scores, many from the 1980s and 1990s that have not been retested, and the pooled hydration result was not significant.
Melatonin recovery evidence is narrow (one antioxidant marker) and based on highly heterogeneous studies.

whatCouldChange.text: Studies of collegiate or female team-sport athletes eating from fixed travel menus across congested weeks could confirm or revise these priorities. The UEFA statement notes limited evidence for nutrition in stressful environments other than heat.
Better-controlled melatonin and polyphenol trials in team-sport athletes could change how supplements are ranked.

evidenceTension.text: A rugby league review lists about 300 mg of polyphenols as potentially improving recovery, yet tart cherry had no effect on soreness, function or inflammation in 11 professional rugby league players, UEFA states evidence does not support tart cherry in football, and a Cochrane review found antioxidants do not meaningfully reduce soreness. On hydration, the review's authors suggest poor rehydration may impair glycogen and next-day performance, but their pooled hydration analysis was not significant, one included study found reduced water content did not impair glycogen resynthesis, and UEFA states normal eating and drinking usually restores euhydration.

claims.text: The UEFA expert group statement on elite football nutrition describes a food first philosophy as fundamental and says evidence must be applied within what is practical and feasible in the football setting.

evidence.excerpt: a ’food first’ philosophy (ie, food over supplements), is fundamental to ensure effective player support.
This requires relevant scientific evidence to be applied according to the constraints of what is practical and feasible in the football setting.

claims.text: The UEFA statement reports that, apart from heat, there is limited evidence for nutritional strategies to support players in stressful environments.

evidence.excerpt: with the exception of heat, there is limited evidence for recommended nutritional strategies to further support players exposed to match demands in stressful environments.

claims.text: For jet lag after travel across time zones, the UEFA statement reports that dietary manipulations of food amount, type, and timing are not unequivocally supported, flags sourcing and side-effect considerations for melatonin, and says pharmacological sleep interventions should be doctor-overseen with sleep hygiene considered first.

evidence.excerpt: Dietary manipulations such as moderating food amount, type and intake patterns have been proposed,188 but the evidence does not support any method unequivocally.208
There are important considerations around the sourcing and side effects of melatonin and readers are directed to a recent review211 for further considerations for travel.
All pharmacological sleep interventions should be overseen by a medical doctor, although sleep hygiene (as part of wider travel hygiene) should always be considered first.

claims.text: The UEFA statement says extreme caution is needed when a sports nutritionist or doctor decides to give supplements to a whole team.

evidence.excerpt: where it may be decided by the sports nutritionist or doctor that supplements should be given to a whole team (either the same mix or a different combination per player), extreme caution must be taken by everyone involved.

claims.text: The UEFA statement notes individual response to nitrate supplementation and the possibility of minor gastrointestinal upset.

evidence.excerpt: Individual response to supplementation. Possibility of minor gastrointestinal upset. Beetroot juice may discolour urine.

claims.text: In its introduction, the hydration and glycogen review cites earlier work reporting that with 1 to 1.2 g/kg/h carbohydrate, about 40% of glycogen is restored in the first hour and about 75% within 4 to 5 hours, and that muscle water is restored within 4 hours if sufficient fluid is ingested.

evidence.excerpt: If sufficient carbohydrates (CHO) are ingested (i.e., 1-1.2 g/kg/h), 40% of glycogen levels can be restored within the first hour of recovery [17,18] and around 75% within 4-5 h postexercise [19].
muscular hydration restorage, which will be totally restored in the 4 h after exercise if sufficient liquid is ingested (1.5 L of the total body weight lost during exercise) [4].

claims.text: In their discussion, the hydration review's authors suggest that poor postexercise rehydration may increase glycogen use in the next session and may decrease performance, especially when high-intensity work is required over consecutive days.

evidence.excerpt: a poor postexercise rehydration strategy may lead to a hypohydrated status, which, in turn, may result in an increased glycogen utilization rate during the subsequent exercise session. This can decrease performance, especially in disciplines where high-intensity performance is required over consecutive days.

claims.text: One study included in the review concluded that reduced water content during the first 15 hours of recovery did not impair muscle glycogen resynthesis.

evidence.excerpt: Neufer et al. [20] concluded that despite reduced water content during the first 15 h of recovery, muscle glycogen resynthesis is not impaired.

claims.text: The review's authors note that many included studies date from the 1980s and 1990s and have not been retested, and that all included studies scored rather low on risk of bias, so results should be taken with caution.

evidence.excerpt: some of the studies included in it are from the past century. Initial studies carried out during the 1980s and 1990s drew conclusions that have not been retested.
all the studies obtained a rather low score, so the results presented should be taken with caution.

claims.text: A review of young professional male rugby league players states that nutrition recommendations should adapt to the frequency and demands of training and match play.

evidence.excerpt: Nutrition recommendations should adapt to different frequencies and demands of training and match play to optimize players’ performance.

claims.text: The rugby league review notes that data may be insufficient for sport-specific recommendations, but suggests players may require about 6 to 8 g/kg/day carbohydrate and 1.6 to 2.6 g/kg/day protein.

evidence.excerpt: Although there may not be enough data to provide RL-speciﬁc recommendations, the available data suggest that players may require approximately 6-8 g·kg−1·day−1 carbohydrate, 1.6-2.6 g·kg−1·day−1 protein,

claims.text: For 80 to 120 kg rugby league players, the review suggests 1 to 4 g/kg carbohydrate plus 0.25 g/kg protein 1 to 4 hours before competition, and 1.0 to 1.5 g/kg carbohydrate plus 0.25 to 0.55 g/kg protein 0 to 2 hours after.

evidence.excerpt: Competition nutrition should maximize glycogen availability by consuming 1-4 g/kg carbohydrate (∼80-320 g) plus 0.25 g/kg (∼20-30 g) protein, 1-4 hr preexercise for 80-120 kg players.
Carbohydrate intakes of approximately 80-180 g (1.0-1.5 g/kg) plus 20-67 g protein (0.25-0.55 g/kg) 0-2 hr postexercise will optimize glycogen resynthesis and muscle protein synthesis.

claims.text: Cited in the rugby league review: in trained cyclists after glycogen-depleting exercise, 1.5 g/kg sucrose, a multiple-transportable carbohydrate, produced lower upper gastrointestinal distress ratings than glucose.

evidence.excerpt: Following glycogen-depleting exercise, trained cyclists presented lower subjective ratings of upper gastrointestinal distress after consuming 1.5 g/kg of sucrose, a multiple-transportable CHO source, than with glucose ingestion (Fuchs et al., 2016).

claims.text: The rugby league review suggests individualization may supersede periodization because players need constantly high energy, carbohydrate, and protein intakes during the season.

evidence.excerpt: Individualization may supersede periodization, per se, given that during an RL season, players require constantly high intakes of energy, CHO, and protein

claims.text: The rugby league review lists caffeine at 3 to 6 mg/kg and about 300 mg polyphenols about 1 hour before exercise among supplements that potentially improve performance, recovery, and adaptation.

evidence.excerpt: Supplements that potentially improve performance, recovery, and adaptation include low to moderate dosages of caffeine (3-6 mg/kg) and ∼300 mg polyphenols consumed ∼1 hr preexercise,

claims.text: A crossover study of 11 professional rugby league players across two matches, described in the review, found tart cherry beverages did not affect muscle soreness, function, or inflammation compared with placebo.

evidence.excerpt: Two, separate 1-week supplementation periods included either tart cherry (2 × 320 mg of anthocyanins) or energy-matched placebo beverages.
Elsewhere, research found that tart cherry did not affect muscle soreness, function, or inﬂammation following two matches in 11 professional RL players.

claims.text: A Cochrane review of 50 studies (1089 mostly male participants, all using above-recommended antioxidant doses) concluded antioxidant supplements and enriched foods are not an effective strategy to reduce soreness, and noted some, such as NAC, may cause gastrointestinal discomfort and diarrhoea.

evidence.excerpt: Some antioxidant supplements such as NAC may cause unwanted side effects including gastrointestinal discomfort and diarrhoea. Thus, taking antioxidant supplements and antioxidant-enriched foods is not an effective strategy to reduce DOMS after exercise.
All studies used an antioxidant dosage higher than the recommended daily amount.

claims.text: A meta-analysis of caffeine studies advises caution with doses above 6 mg/kg because, in the few studies available, they did not show added benefit and may increase side effects, and found pre-competition caffeine withdrawal unnecessary.

evidence.excerpt: It would be wise to be cautious about ingesting high doses of caffeine (> 6 mg/kg BM) before exercise, as this does not appear to have an additional ergogenic effect and may increase the risk of undesired side effects.
these data suggest that pre-competition caffeine withdrawal is unnecessary to elicit a performance-enhancing effect from pre-exercise caffeine supplementation.

claims.text: A meta-analysis of melatonin studies concluded melatonin is not ergogenic. Its reported recovery benefit rested on an increase in one antioxidant marker, glutathione peroxidase.

evidence.excerpt: The data indicate that melatonin is not an ergogenic hormone. In contrast, melatonin supplementation improves post-exercise recovery, even without altering its secretion.
Only Glutathione Peroxidase (GPx) secretion increased after melatonin supplementation (1.40; 95% CI: 0.29 to 2.51).

claims.text: The melatonin meta-analysis authors state their conclusions came from highly heterogeneous studies and further evidence is needed.

evidence.excerpt: These conclusions were based on studies with high heterogeneity, suggesting that further evidence is necessary to establish the physiological role of melatonin on exercise performance and recovery in humans.

claims.text: In professional male rugby union players, overnight long-haul travel caused about 3 hours of in-flight sleep loss, likely explaining immediate declines in physical and cognitive performance. The authors recommend scheduling departures and arrivals to minimize sleep disruption.

evidence.excerpt: Overnight long-haul travel induces partial sleep deprivation (∼3 h in-ﬂight, as seen in both part I and part II), likely explaining the immediate deterioration in physical and cognitive performance of professional rugby union players.
Accordingly, teams should schedule departure and arrival times that minimize sleep disruption to preserve physical and cognitive performance for matches.

claims.text: In 68 male national-team footballers, daytime arrivals (11 AM to 5 PM) were least detrimental to perceived sleep and fatigue ratings, and the authors note adequate sleep on the night of arrival is important.

evidence.excerpt: Daytime arrivals (11 AM to 5 PM) were the least detrimental to sleep and fatigue ratings and where possible trips should be scheduled to arrive during the day.
ensuring athletes are provided with adequate sleep on the night of arrival is important.

claims.text: In 24 professional male outfield soccer players from one reserve team, players with more match playing time had higher accumulated weekly load (training plus match) for most external load variables.

evidence.excerpt: players (as a whole o per demarcation) with more match playing time had a higher accumulative weekly load for most of the variables,

claims.text: The Australian football case-report authors recommend sufficient dietary carbohydrate, likely above 6 g/kg, in the 24 hours before match play.

evidence.excerpt: sport physiologists and nutritionists should ensure that AF players consume sufﬁcient dietary CHO intake (likely >6 g/kg) in the 24 hours prior to participation in match play.

claims.text: For injured players, the UEFA statement recommends daily protein of at least 1.6 g/kg during rehabilitation and moving back toward normal training nutrition as the player progresses toward return to play.

evidence.excerpt: with the resultant recommended daily protein intake being ≥1.6 g/kg BM

move back towards nutritional recommendations to support optimal training performance and adaptations (detailed in the section ‘Expert group topic 2’) as the player moves along the spectrum of return to play

claims.text: The UEFA statement reports that a recent football study found no improvement in recovery markers or soreness with tart cherry juice and concludes evidence does not support its specific use in football.

evidence.excerpt: recent investigation in football did not show improved recovery markers of function or subjective soreness.78 Therefore, the available evidence does not support its specific use in football.

claims.text: The rugby league review notes possible caffeine side effects including sleep disturbances and anxiety. The caffeine meta-analysis authors also cite IOC guidance that high doses may increase the risk of insomnia and other side effects.

evidence.excerpt: taking caution to possible side effects, such as sleep disturbances and anxiety, possibly inﬂuenced by genetic predispositions
the intake of high doses of caffeine may increase the risk of side effects, such as nausea, anxiety, insomnia, and restlessness

claims.text: In the rugby union travel study, physical performance stayed impaired for 3 mornings after arrival despite restored sleep (+1 time zone), and the authors recommend arriving more than 3 days before matches after overnight long-haul journeys.

evidence.excerpt: While sleep was restored on the ﬁrst night after travel, physical performance remained impaired for 3 mornings on arrival (+1 time zone; part I).
For teams undertaking overnight long-haul journeys for competition, it is recommended to arrive more than 3 days before matches to enable sufﬁcient physical and cognitive recovery

claims.text: The UEFA statement says carbohydrate intake should stay at 6 to 8 g/kg/day for the 48 to 72 hours between congested fixtures, while noting players often eat closer to about 4 g/kg.

evidence.excerpt: Where the match schedule consists of congested fixtures (eg, domestic fixtures, European competition, international games), CHO intake should be maintained within this range (6-8 g/kg BM/day) for the 48-72 hours between games to promote adequate glycogen storage.
The reality is that players often consume less than this and daily intake may be closer to about 4 g/kg BM.

claims.text: Drawing on an English Premier League study of a week with two games and five training days, the UEFA statement suggests raising carbohydrate to 6 to 8 g/kg on the day before, day of, and day after a match.

evidence.excerpt: microcycle consisting of two games and five training days
it is suggested that players should increase CHO intake on MD-1, MD and MD +1 to between 6 and 8 g/kg BM

claims.text: The UEFA statement advises an easily digestible pre-match meal, prioritising comfort over rigid carbohydrate targets, and practising all match nutrition strategies, including sports foods, in training and minor matches to identify adverse effects.

evidence.excerpt: should be easily digestible to reduce the risk of gastrointestinal problems (eg, reflux, discomfort)
so comfort should be considered, rather than rigid strategies focused solely on meeting CHO intake guidelines

All match nutrition strategies, including the use of supplements (eg, sports foods), should be practised in training and minor matches to allow individualised protocols to be developed and to identify adverse effects in players

claims.text: The UEFA statement warns that food storage and preparation at postmatch buffets, including in the changing room or team bus, can cause serious gastrointestinal illness, and points to hygiene controls covering cross-contamination, cleaning, chilling and cooking.

evidence.excerpt: serious gastrointestinal illness caused by bacterial contamination may occur in relation to the storage and preparation of food consumed in training ground restaurants or venues used for postmatch buffets (eg, the changing room or team bus).
contamination, cleaning, chilling and cooking. Resources that address these ‘4 Cs’, including hygiene training documents and videos

claims.text: The UEFA statement describes itself as level 5 (expert opinion) evidence.

evidence.excerpt: The reader should note that this expert group statement represents level 5 (expert opinion) evidence.

claims.text: The UEFA statement suggests postmatch meals and snacks target about 1 g/kg/h carbohydrate for 4 hours, and notes sports foods can help when appetite is reduced or food is sourced away from home.

evidence.excerpt: Postmatch meals and snacks should target a CHO intake of ~1 g/kg BM/hour for 4 hours
Sports foods may provide a preferred option to supply macronutrients, especially to achieve CHO guidelines when appetite may be reduced or when sourcing food away from the home environment.

claims.text: The UEFA statement says sweat rates vary greatly between players, that planning around individual sweat losses can meet each player's needs, and that in most situations normal eating and drinking restores euhydration after a match.

evidence.excerpt: Sweat rates vary greatly between players and are primarily influenced by the intensity of exercise, environmental conditions and acclimation status.
some forward planning (eg, understanding individual sweat losses, developing individualised hydration plans, alongside player education) can ensure that each player’s hydration needs are met
in most situations there is sufficient opportunity and time to restore euhydration and electrolyte balance with normal eating/drinking practices

claims.text: Citing ACSM guidance, the rugby league review advises keeping fluid losses under 2% of body mass during training and competition and drinking about 1.25 to 1.5 L per kg of body mass lost after exercise.

evidence.excerpt: During training and competition, athletes need to avoid ﬂuid losses that exceed 2% BM (i.e., players weighing 80-100 kg should not lose >1.6-2.0/kg BM) to prevent dehydration
Postexercise, players should consume approximately 1.25-1.5 L·kg−1·BM−1 lost (Sawka et al., 2007) to ensure adequate rehydration.

claims.text: In the context of limiting illness risk, the UEFA statement says a broad multivitamin and mineral supplement is the best choice to support food intake when food choice and quality may be limited.

evidence.excerpt: multivitamin/mineral supplement is the best choice to support food intake in situations where food choices and quality may be limited

assumptions: Time zones crossed and travel mode are unknown, so jet lag and long-haul travel findings may or may not apply.
Returning athletes are assumed to be returning from injury or reduced training, with clinical oversight already in place.
The two competitions are assumed to be separated by a few days, making early post-competition recovery relevant.
coverageGaps: No source tests a nutrition plan across a congested collegiate travel week with fixed hotel meals and limited refrigeration; UEFA guidance on congested fixtures and food hygiene is expert opinion
No source tests fueling for athletes returning to play within a congested competition week; UEFA gives only general rehabilitation guidance
No source tests how caffeine dose or timing affects athletes' sleep; sources only list sleep disturbance and insomnia as possible side effects
No female or collegiate team-sport data on individualized sweat-rate based hydration during travel
